desc:
Cut the string s into consecutive non-empty pieces (their concatenation must be exactly s) such that no two pieces are equal strings. Return the largest number of pieces that such a cut can have.

For example, "ababccc" can be cut into a|b|ab|c|cc, which has 5 distinct pieces; 6 pieces are impossible.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
hints: At each position you decide where the current piece ends. A set of pieces used so far tells you which choices are forbidden.
Recurse on the start index with a set of used pieces. Try every end index, skip a piece already in the set, add it, recurse, remove it. Track the best count when the end of the string is reached.
Prune: if the pieces so far plus the number of characters left (the absolute maximum number of further pieces) cannot beat the best answer found, stop.
editorial: Backtracking on the cut positions. State: index i where the next piece starts, the number of pieces so far, and the set of pieces already used. For each end j > i, the candidate piece is s[i:j]. If it is not in the set, add it, recurse with j, and remove it again. When i == n, record the piece count.

There are 2n-1 ways to cut a string of length n, so exploring everything costs at most about that many nodes, which is acceptable for n ≤ 20. A strong and cheap prune is the bound count + (n - i) ≤ best: every remaining character can become at most one more piece, so if that cannot exceed the current best the branch is useless.
The set must be updated and restored symmetrically (add before the recursive call, remove after). Forgetting to remove is the classic bug in this kind of search.
